content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta, USA, contributed to the guidelines through the involvement of Lindley Barbee, who serves as the Clinical Team Lead in the Division of STD Prevention. Azadeh Baghaki, Strategy Manager at Unitaid in Geneva, Switzerland, also participated in the development process. Francis Kakooza, Head of the Global Health Security Department at the Infectious Diseases Institute, Makerere University, Kampala, Uganda, provided expertise. Fernando Pascal Martinez, Research and Development Access Development Lead at the Global Antibiotic Research and Development Partnership in Barcelona, Spain, contributed as well. Tim Sladden, Senior Advisor for Sexual and Reproductive Health at the United Nations Population Fund in New York, USA, was another key participant. The Methodologist and Evidence Review Team included Maria Ximena Rojas Reyes from the Institut d’Recerca, Hospital de la Santa Creu i Sant Pau, Barcelona, Spain. For treatment recommendations, the systematic review team was led by Nancy Santesso, with contributions from Angela Barbara and Meha Bhatt, all affiliated with the Michael G. DeGroote Cochrane Canada Centre at McMaster University, Hamilton, Canada. For syphilis testing, Jason Ong led the team, which included Eric Chow, Christopher Fairley, Su Mei Goh, Janet Towns, Warittha Tieosapjareon, and Ying Zhang, all from Monash University and the Melbourne Sexual Health Centre in Melbourne, Australia. For partner services, Nicholas Henschke from Cochrane Response in Heidelberg, Germany, and Michael Marks from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, United Kingdom, contributed. Oriol Mitjà from the Fight AIDS and Infectious Disease Foundation in Barcelona, Spain, Minh Duc Pham from the Burnet Institute in Melbourne, Australia, and Gemma Villanueva from Cochrane Response in London, United Kingdom, also participated. The WHO Secretariat and Steering Committee members based at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, included Avni Amin, Technical Officer in the Department of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research (SRH); Kingsley Asiedu, Medical Officer in the Department of Neglected Tropical Diseases; Rachel Baggaley, Unit Head for Testing, Prevention, and Populations in the Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infection Programmes (HHS); Magdalena Barr-DiChiara, Technical Officer in the Department of HHS; Maeve Brito de Mello, Technical Officer in the Department of HHS; Peter Cherutich, Consultant in the Department of HHS; Meg Doherty, Director of the Department of HHS; Sami Gottlieb, Medical Officer in the Department of SRH; Benedikt Huttner, Team Lead in the Department of Access to Medicines and Health Products; Cheryl Johnson, Technical Officer in the Department of HHS; James Kiarie, Unit Head in the Department of SRH; Mark Lanigan, Technical Officer for Regulation and Prequalification; and others. The updated recommendations address the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and syphilis, as well as new recommendations for syphilis testing and partner services. These updates were developed with input from a wide range of experts, including those from WHO regional offices and external review groups. The contributors declared their interests and potential conflicts, which were managed appropriately to ensure the integrity of the guideline development process. For example, Catherine Ngugi from the Ministry of Health in Kenya declared research support from the Global Antibiotic Research and Development Partnership (GARDP) and the Drugs for Neglected Diseases Initiative (DNDi) for a study on the prevalence of C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae infections among pregnant women and key populations in Kenya. Similarly, Remco Peters from the University of Pretoria, South Africa, declared research support from the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND) for evaluating a lateral flow assay for point-of-care detection of N. gonorrhoeae. The guidelines were developed with full participation from experts across various institutions, including the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, the University of Melbourne, the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Belgium, and others. Observers and external reviewers also contributed to the process, ensuring a comprehensive and evidence-based approach to updating STI treatment recommendations.
